weeks.title: Week ending Aug 2, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week orbited one big question: is the AI capex boom rational, and who pays when it isn't? You read bottoms-up bulls (a breakeven model showing Google's cloud capex covers its cost of capital 3x over; Jamin Ball's cloud run-rates accelerating across AWS, Azure, and GCP) against a growing bear file: South Korea's memory-stock crash wiping $1.2 trillion, Leopold Aschenbrenner's leveraged AI fund going hat-in-hand after a 439% first half, 'spend now, lease later' data-center financing, hidden RSU compensation costs eroding Meta's real margins, and hyperscaler credit spreads widening under $165B of AI bond supply. The credit plumbing got its own thread — securitisation's embedded leverage, private credit's entanglement with insurance, and MBS convexity — with practitioners like Scott Goodwin noting there's 'too much discourse about AI but not enough about leverage.'

Running underneath it all is the book you're reading: Liaquat Ahamed's '1873', where railroad bonds played the role AI data-center debt plays today — a transformative technology, financed by retail-distributed paper and high-pressure salesmanship, that still produced the worst corporate default wave in American history. Your highlights (Jay Cooke's bond campaign, the dismissed warning about 'handsomely engraved railroad bonds', a third of railway bonds in receivership) read like annotations on this week's news.

Around the edges: Paul Graham on great work and real persistence, a frontier-lab agent intrusion post-mortem that doubles as a warning about autonomous-agent security, the political economy of supply chains and Iran, and craft-versus-automation tensions in coding education and AI-era design aesthetics.

lessons_learned.lesson: Separate the returns math from the financing structure. Google's capex clears its cost of capital 3x over, yet the week's blowups (Korea's leveraged single-stock ETFs, Aschenbrenner's fund) were all financing-structure failures, not unit-economics failures. When you evaluate the AI buildout, ask 'who is levered to this?' before 'is it profitable?'

lessons_learned.lesson: Structure hides risk multipliers: an ABS equity tranche can lose 33x what a pro-rata investor loses on identical defaults, and 'performs until it does not' applies to every structured product you'll be pitched. Read the tranche, not the headline yield.

sources.title: The dark arts of securitisation

lessons_learned.lesson: Watch for risk being socialized before the loss event, not after. Private credit routing through insurance balance sheets means taxpayers may already be the implicit backstop — the 2008 lesson (find where risk pools quietly) applies now, in a different wrapper.

sources.title: Why Private Credit Got Entangled With Insurance

lessons_learned.lesson: Check reported profitability for costs routed around the income statement: Meta funding AI-talent RSUs via buybacks may overstate EBIT margin by ~10 points. When a company is in an arms race, ask what the race costs that the P&L doesn't show.

sources.title: The hidden financial costs of chasing AI supremacy

lessons_learned.lesson: History's template for this moment is 1873, not 1929: transformative infrastructure (railroads/data centers), financed by aggressively-sold paper, warnings dismissed as unimaginative — then a default wave worse than the Great Depression's. The tech was real; the paper still defaulted. Both things were true.

lessons_learned.lesson: Persistence is attachment to goals, not methods — Graham's distinction between the persistent (open to feedback, flexible on approach) and the obstinate (rigid on approach) is a practical test you can apply to your own projects this week.

lessons_learned.lesson: Measure AI adoption by business outcomes, not activity metrics: Coinbase's 2.5x pull requests per engineer with lower revenue and falling net income is the cleanest cautionary datapoint yet against celebrating productivity proxies.

contrarian_insights.insight: The hyperscaler credit-spread panic is a supply story, not a solvency story: $165B of AI-linked bond issuance in H1 widened spreads mechanically, making long hyperscaler credit a buy once supply clears — the opposite of the consensus 'credit stress' read. The tell to watch: hyperscaler OAS converging with junk would break this thesis.

source.title: Wild Beast and Fickle, Too: Market is Misreading Hyperscaler Spreads

contrarian_insights.insight: More reasoning does not mean better decisions: across a 2-year backtest, no state-of-the-art LLM beat a simple static baseline at trading, and dialing up reasoning effort didn't help — models traded less when losing rather than better. A direct counter to 'scale reasoning, get alpha.'

The 1873 panic was arguably a *good* crash: losses exceeding 7% of GDP were largely confined to the wealthy investor class — a 'rich man's panic' — which challenges the assumption that every financial crisis must be socialized to protect the real economy.

Substack is being killed by its growth features: adding Notes, video, and free content accelerated subscription fatigue and eroded paid revenue even as engagement rose — engagement growth and creator income can move in opposite directions.

source.title: The Real Reason that Substack is Collapsing

contrarian_insights.insight: 'The market is doing the Fed's job' may be exactly backwards as policy: Warsh implying market-driven rate rises can substitute for hikes injects an uncertainty premium that is neither controllable nor coherent — and Weisenthal's blunt take says anyone repeating the phrase is confused.

source.title: Trying to make sense of Warsh

contrarian_insights.insight: Countries don't choose monetary standards on economic logic: Germany went to gold 'not because gold is gold, but because Britain is Britain' — prestige mimicry, not optimization. Worth remembering whenever 'inevitable' monetary regimes (then gold, now dollar or crypto) are debated.

book_progress.author: Liaquat Ahamed
book_progress.note: Eight highlights this week, moving from the front matter into the run-up to the Panic: Jay Cooke recycling his Civil War retail-bond playbook to push Northern Pacific paper (p.133), a contemporary warning about railroad bonds 'going to protest' that was dismissed, the staggering claim that 1874–76 saw worse corporate default rates than the Great Depression (p.153), and Bamberger's confession that Germany chose gold for prestige, not economics. The book is functioning as a lens for the week's AI-capex reading: transformative infrastructure, aggressive financing, dismissed skeptics.

weeks.title: Week ending Aug 9, 2026
weeks.overview:
Your reading this week split into two dominant currents that kept crossing paths: the AI infrastructure supercycle and the plumbing of sovereign finance. On the AI side, you moved from macro (hyperscaler credit spreads, SoftBank's leveraged bet on OpenAI, Nvidia quietly cutting Rubin Ultra memory specs) down to the research layer (Lilian Weng's harness-engineering survey, Anthropic's discovery of a "global workspace" inside Claude, Ankur Goyal's point about judging agents on behavior rather than output) and back up to strategy (O'Reilly's read on Google's DeepMind shakeup as a deliberate Westinghouse-style diffusion play, reinforced by Jeffrey Ding's book on why diffusion — not invention — wins great-power tech races). The throughline is that the AI story is quietly shifting from "who has the best model" to "who controls the supply chain, the scaffolding, and the distribution," with real financial strain (Datadog's customer pullback, Nvidia's memory shortage, SoftBank's borrowing-against-stake maneuver) showing the capex boom isn't frictionless.

The second thread was sovereign and monetary plumbing under stress: Ethiopia's value recovery instruments, the Brady Plan's lessons for today's Common Framework debt restructurings, the BoJ's carry-trade trap, the US-Japan yen intervention, and the shift of Treasury yield price discovery away from FOMC meeting days. These pieces share a skepticism of institutional machinery — VRIs get gamed, the Common Framework lacks the Brady Plan's political coordination, and central banks are reaching for increasingly unconventional tools (repo facilities, euro sales, staggered lock-ups) because the old playbooks no longer fit. A smaller but sharp third thread ran through geopolitics-as-economics: tungsten as a war-prediction market, Hadrian's Wall as a monument to imperial overreach, and the Iran-Oman Strait of Hormuz toll idea, all treating hard-power questions through a market lens.

Your book highlights this week tracked closely with the money themes: The Almighty Dollar's account of the Joachimsthal silver boom reads like a 16th-century startup case study, and its closing highlight — that Toledo/Spain collapsed *because of* silver abundance, not despite it — is a striking echo of this week's supply-glut argument about hyperscaler bonds and the risk of AI capex oversupply.

book_progress.book: The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World's Most Powerful Money
book_progress.author: Brendan Greeley
book_progress.note: This week's highlights follow the book's origin story at Joachimsthal, the 16th-century Bohemian silver-mining town Greeley reframes in deliberately sardonic startup language — a monetary historian even calls it a 'Silicon Valley' of joint-stock capital, and Greeley narrates its IPO-style hype party as 'always an indicator that the founders have gotten ahead of themselves.' The arc lands on the book's central paradox by page 70: Toledo, and by extension Spain, didn't collapse despite an abundance of silver dollars — it collapsed because of them. That's a striking echo of this week's articles on the AI-bond supply glut and SoftBank's leverage-on-leverage bet: abundance and overextension, not scarcity, are what tend to break systems. (A parallel thread from 1873: The Rothschilds also ran this week, tracing Grant-era hero-worship and gift-showering as the excess that preceded the 1873 crash — the same abundance-precedes-collapse pattern from a different century.)
